def: The unit of caching and coherence in a CPU cache, 64 bytes on mainstream servers (implementation-dependent). An aligned 64-byte NVMe SQE occupies exactly one line.
Hardware keeping all caches and memory consistent; for I/O, coherent DMA means the platform snoops CPU caches on device reads and invalidates stale lines on device writes.
CPU attribute of an address range that sets caching and ordering rules: write-back (DRAM), uncached (device registers such as NVMe doorbells), write-combining (frame buffers, some CMB data).
Per-core queue in which retired stores wait before becoming visible to other agents; a source of observable reordering that barriers constrain.
Instruction or primitive constraining the order in which memory operations become visible (e.g. x86 sfence, Arm dmb; Linux wmb, dma_wmb). Linux writel() includes the ordering a doorbell write needs.
Memory and PCIe Root Ports attached to particular sockets; access from another socket crosses an inter-socket link and is slower. A PCI device reports its home node in sysfs numa_node.
The set of CPUs an interrupt vector is steered to; Linux NVMe uses kernel-managed affinity with one completion vector per CPU group.
Access to device registers through loads and stores to physical addresses claimed by a BAR; stores become posted Memory Writes, loads become non-posted Memory Reads the CPU waits for.
The address a driver gives a device for DMA: an IOVA when an IOMMU translates, otherwise a physical (bus) address.
A set of IOMMU page tables defining one I/O virtual address space; all devices attached to the domain share it.
The smallest set of PCI functions the platform can isolate from one another; VFIO assigns whole groups. Shaped by topology and ACS.
Cache of recent IOMMU translations; a miss costs a page walk in DRAM, and unmapping requires invalidating it.
The number of address bits a device can generate, set by the driver (e.g. dma_set_mask_and_coherent); too small a mask forces bounce buffering or low IOVAs.
Linux bounce-buffer pool the device can reach; the CPU copies data between it and the real buffer. Used for limited DMA masks and some confidential-computing guests.
PCIe mechanism by which a device requests translations from the translation agent (IOMMU), caches them in its ATC and issues translated requests (AT=10b); unmapping requires ATS invalidation.
The device-side cache of translations obtained through ATS; must be invalidated (Invalidate Request / Invalidate Completion messages) when mappings change.
PCIe mechanism (with ATS) by which a device asks the host to make non-resident pages present; answered by a PRG Response message.
A 20-bit identifier attached to a request selecting one of several address spaces within a single function; used for shared virtual addressing.
The part of a PCIe hierarchy below one Root Port; routing between hierarchy domains happens inside the Root Complex and peer-to-peer between them is optional.
Base/limit range in a Type 1 header that a bridge forwards downstream: memory (32-bit, 1 MiB granularity), prefetchable memory (optionally 64-bit) and I/O (4 KiB granularity).
Forwarding of memory and I/O requests by comparing their address with bridge windows.
Forwarding by Bus/Device/Function compared with secondary/subordinate bus ranges; used for completions, configuration requests and ID-routed messages.
Message routing determined by the message type: routed to the Root Complex, broadcast from it, local, or gathered and routed to it.
A PCIe requester targeting another device's BAR instead of host memory; switch-local unless ACS redirects it, and optional between Root Ports.

PCIe extended capability with per-port controls (Source Validation, Translation Blocking, P2P Request/Completion Redirect, Upstream Forwarding, P2P Egress Control, Direct Translated P2P) that steer traffic where the IOMMU can check it.
An Endpoint built into the Root Complex, with no link of its own.
A Root Complex function that collects error and PME messages from Root Complex Integrated Endpoints.
An independent 256-bus configuration space, the leading 0000 in 0000:01:00.0; large systems have several.
A component with one upstream port and several downstream ports, each presented to software as a Type 1 bridge on an internal virtual bus.
Discovering a BAR's size and type by writing all ones and reading back the writable bits (both halves for a 64-bit BAR), with decoding disabled.
Placing a block of size S at an address that is a multiple of S; required for BARs.
An address range the Root Complex forwards to PCIe, reported by firmware (ACPI _CRS); every Root Port window must fit inside one.
Firmware setting that provides a 64-bit host-bridge aperture so 64-bit prefetchable BARs and windows can be placed above 4 GiB.
Bus numbers and window space set aside below hot-plug-capable ports so devices added later can be assigned resources.
ACPI method through which the OS requests control of native PCIe features such as hot-plug, AER, PME, LTR and DPC.
Linux sysfs operations that re-enumerate a bus or remove a function; state-changing, for test systems.
Reinterprets the device and function fields of a Routing ID as an 8-bit function number for the device below a port; requires ARI Forwarding Enable in the Downstream Port.
PCIe capability letting a Physical Function create Virtual Functions with their own Routing IDs (from First VF Offset and VF Stride) and BAR space.
Completion status meaning 'not ready, retry'; renamed Request Retry Status in recent revisions. With CRS Software Visibility, a Vendor ID read returns 0001h.
Register attribute: hardware sets the bit, software clears it by writing 1; writing 0 has no effect. Writing back a read value clears every set bit.
A register bit not reinitialized by resets that preserve sticky state (subject to auxiliary power); AER status bits are sticky, so they can show errors from before the current boot.
Register attribute: set by hardware or firmware at initialization, read-only to software afterwards.
Reserved register bits that software must write back with the value it read.
Reserved register bits that software must write as zero.
TLP header fields selecting which bytes of the first and last DWORD are accessed; configuration requests use only First DW BE.
A structure in configuration space from offset 100h with a header of ID [15:0], version [19:16] and next offset [31:20]; an all-zero header at 100h means none exist.
Extended capability (ID 0023h) whose content is defined by the organization named by its designated vendor ID and DVSEC ID.
Reset of a single function initiated through Device Control; non-sticky configuration returns to defaults, so software must restore saved state.
